summaries.example: Imagine making a clay bowl. The clay answers “What is it made from?” The bowl’s shape answers “What is it?” The potter’s skill explains what starts the change. The bowl’s use explains what the work is for. Aristotle says a good explanation can include all four answers.
summaries.summary: Aristotle asks what it means to really understand something. He says understanding requires knowing its cause, meaning an appropriate answer to why it is the way it is. He describes four kinds of causes. The material cause is what something is made from. The formal cause is what kind of thing it is or what shape it has. The efficient cause is what brings about a change. The final cause is what something is for or what good it serves. A bronze statue, for example, needs the bronze, its shape, the craft that makes it, and the statue as the goal of the work. Aristotle also applies these ideas to nature. He thinks the parts of animals often have roles that help the animal live or flourish. He does not say every event has all four causes. His example of a lunar eclipse shows that some events may lack a final cause or a strict material cause. The important lesson is that careful investigation looks for the kinds of causes that truly explain the thing.
key_ideas: Aristotle thinks learning means finding the right answer to a “why?” question.
He describes four kinds of causes: material, formal, efficient, and final.
A full explanation may need several causes, not just one.
For living things, Aristotle gives special importance to what their parts are for.
He says regular patterns in nature should not be dismissed as mere coincidence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s idea reminds us that “What happened?” is not the only question worth asking. We can also ask what something is made of, what kind of thing it is, what produced it, and what role or end it has. Thinking this way can help us give clearer explanations instead of stopping at the first answer.

important_terms.definition: An answer to a “why?” question. Aristotle thinks different kinds of answers may explain the same thing.
The stuff something is made from, such as clay in a clay bowl.
The shape or kind of thing something is; for example, being a bowl rather than a lump of clay.
What brings about a change, such as a craft or process that makes something.
The end, use, or good that something is for.
An explanation that refers to an end or goal.

questions_to_think_about: When you explain how something was made, which of the four causes do you mention?
Can one thing have more than one useful explanation?
Why might regular patterns in nature need an explanation?
Is something’s purpose always the same as the reason a person wanted it?

summaries.example: Consider a lunar eclipse. The moon is the subject that undergoes the change, though Aristotle says it is not literally the eclipse’s matter. The proximate efficient cause is the earth’s coming between the sun and moon, blocking the light. Aristotle says the eclipse has no final cause. This case shows that the four causes are a framework of possible explanatory roles, not a checklist that every event must satisfy.
summaries.summary: Aristotle develops a theory of causality because he regards science as the search for well-grounded answers to why-questions. A cause is not limited to a force that pushes an event. It is an explanatory role played by something in relation to what is being explained. The four primary roles are material, formal, efficient, and final. In producing a bronze statue, bronze is the material, the statue’s shape is formal, the relevant bronze-casting craft is efficient, and the finished statue is the end. Aristotle’s choice of the craft rather than simply the artisan is meant to identify what generally explains the production process, although particular explanations may also refer to an individual maker. Causes must be intrinsic: a description such as “the artisan’s being someone’s daughter” may be true but does not explain how the statue was produced. In natural science, all four kinds may be relevant to natural change, though not every individual event has every kind. Aristotle defends final causality by arguing that material processes alone do not explain the stable connection between an organism’s parts and its needs. His argument is presented as the best explanation of regularity, not as a strict proof by itself. Matter is then understood through hypothetical necessity: given an end, certain material conditions are required. Aristotle also gives final/formal causes explanatory priority in natural generation while retaining the need for the other causes. The eclipse example shows the flexibility of the framework: its proximate efficient cause is the earth’s interposition, while it lacks a final cause. Causal knowledge therefore requires both identifying relevant kinds and stating them with precision.
key_ideas: Aristotle treats causal inquiry as central to scientific knowledge: to know a thing is to grasp its relevant cause or why.
His causal pluralism holds that four irreducible explanatory roles may apply: material, formal, efficient, and final.
The causes must be described accurately and intrinsically; merely naming an associated person or circumstance is not enough.
In natural science, matter and efficient processes matter, but Aristotle argues that regular organization also calls for final-causal explanation.
Final and formal causes often coincide in natural generation and can have explanatory priority over the initiating efficient cause.

The theory is not a universal four-part checklist: a lunar eclipse illustrates that some phenomena lack a final cause and have only an analogous underlying subject rather than matter strictly speaking.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s account challenges a narrow picture of explanation as identifying only a prior event. It asks investigators to distinguish what a thing is made of, what structure it has, what produces it, and what role or end organizes the process. It also raises a lasting methodological question: when regularity and function appear together in nature, can a purely material account explain their connection, or is a teleological account needed? Even where one rejects Aristotle’s conclusions, these distinctions clarify what different explanations are trying to accomplish.

important_terms.definition: A cause understood as an explanatory factor: an answer to the relevant “why?” question about a thing or change.
The underlying material or subject involved in something’s production or change.
The essence, structure, or form that makes something the kind of thing it is.
The source or principle from which a change begins; Aristotle may identify a craft or process rather than merely naming an individual agent.
That for the sake of which something occurs: an end understood in relation to what is good for the relevant thing.
An account that explains a process by reference to its end or function, without necessarily appealing to an agent’s intentions.
Material conditions that are necessary if a certain end is to be realized; they are explained in relation to that end.
A factor that happens to be associated with an outcome but does not explain it. Aristotle contrasts this with an intrinsic cause.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining regular biological organization require more than describing material processes?
Why does Aristotle distinguish the craft of bronze-casting from the individual artisan as an efficient cause in a general explanation?
Does showing that material and efficient causes alone leave regularity unexplained prove that final causes exist, or only support them as an explanation?
How can the final cause be explanatory priority without eliminating the other causes?
What is gained by distinguishing an intrinsic cause from a coincidental association?

summaries.example: Suppose a school makes a wooden desk. The wood is the material cause. Its desk-shape is the formal cause. The woodworking skill and making process are the efficient cause. Its purpose—giving someone a place to work—is the final cause. Saying “the desk was made by the principal’s cousin” may be true, but unless that fact explains the making, it is only a coincidence from Aristotle’s point of view.
summaries.summary: Aristotle believes that science is mainly an investigation of causes. For him, knowing something well means knowing why it is the way it is. He organizes explanations into four kinds. The material cause is what a thing is made from. The formal cause is its structure or defining kind. The efficient cause is what brings about its change. The final cause is the end or good for which it exists or develops. These are not four competing answers where only one can be correct. Several can explain one thing at the same time. Aristotle uses the making of a bronze statue to show this. The bronze, the statue’s shape, the bronze-casting craft, and the finished statue each play a different explanatory role. He also distinguishes genuine causes from coincidences. The artisan’s family relationship, for example, does not explain the statue unless it is relevant to the making. Aristotle applies the framework to nature. He argues that natural science should consider matter, form, what produces change, and the end toward which a process is organized. He especially defends final causes in living things. Sharp front teeth and broad back teeth regularly fit different tasks, such as tearing and grinding food. Aristotle says that simply calling this a lucky coincidence leaves the regular connection unexplained. His argument supports final causality as the best explanation of this feature, though the source notes that it is not a strict proof by itself. Material conditions still matter: they are necessary when a particular end is to be achieved. Finally, Aristotle says final and formal causes can be explanatory priorities without replacing the other causes. key_ideas: Aristotle connects real knowledge with knowing the relevant cause or explanation.
The four causes answer four different questions: made of what, what is it, what changed it, and what is it for?
More than one cause can explain the same thing, and the causes work together.
Aristotle thinks nature’s repeated patterns, especially in living things, are not adequately explained by luck alone.
He gives final causes an important role, but he still keeps material and efficient causes.
Not every event has all four causes; a lunar eclipse is one example Aristotle uses to show this.
summaries.why_it_matters: The four causes teach us to make explanations more complete and precise. A question about how something happens may differ from a question about what it is, what it is made of, or what role it serves. Aristotle’s theory also introduces a debate that still matters: should nature be explained only through matter and motion, or do function and organization require another kind of explanation? Understanding his distinctions helps us discuss that debate carefully.

important_terms.definition: An explanation that answers an important “why?” question about something.
What a thing is made from, such as wood in a desk.
The shape, structure, or kind of thing something is.
What produces a change, especially the skill or process that makes something happen.
The purpose, result, or good for the sake of which something happens.
Explaining something by connecting it with an end, role, or goal.
A condition that must be present if a certain end is to happen.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between a cause and something that merely happens to be connected with an event?
Could a desk’s purpose help explain how its parts are arranged?
Why might Aristotle think animal teeth need a purpose-based explanation?
When does an explanation need several causes rather than one?
Does Aristotle’s argument for final causes prove them, or give a reason to prefer them?
